intro: The Barcarolle is a boat song of 1894, a swaying figure in the right hand under a tune in the left. His only disc recording of it was made for Edison in 1919. Listen for the hush of the middle, the Presto that swells to a loud climax, and the return of the tune afterwards.
question: How does a pianist keep a rocking rhythm going through a climax and back?

Allegro moderato · the tune returns

cues.title: A sway, then a tune below
cues.text: The Moderato is marked pp, with two flats in the key signature. After two bars of the right hand alone, swaying in repeated thirds, the left hand enters with the tune at mf, in its low register.
cues.evidence: The Piano Street scan shows Moderato, pp, a two-flat signature, two opening bars with left-hand rests and a left-hand melody marked mf from bar 3 (https://www.pianostreet.com/rachmaninoff-sheet-music/7-morceaux-de-salon-op-10/barcarolle-op-10-no-3.htm). The analysis puts the file’s global key at G minor (r = 0.83) and the opening among its quietest windows.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Third of seven salon pieces
cues.text: The Barcarolle is the third of the seven Morceaux de salon, Op. 10, composed in 1894. The set also holds a Nocturne, a Valse and a Humoresque, which he recorded for Victor in 1940.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia dates Op. 10 to 1894 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morceaux_de_salon,_Op._10_(Rachmaninoff)); IMSLP’s Op. 10 page lists Nocturne, Valse, Barcarolle and Humoresque among its pieces (https://imslp.org/wiki/7_Morceaux_de_salon,_Op.10_(Rachmaninoff,_Sergei)); the RCA booklet’s discography lists the Humoresque, Op. 10 No. 5, recorded 9 April 1940.

cues.title: A quick figure at ppp
cues.text: Around 1:10 the score marks Con moto: a quick sixteenth-note figure at ppp, marked leggiero, over a held chord. The record stays soft until about 1:35, then builds to a loud stretch by 1:45.
cues.evidence: The score’s third page ends with Con moto, ppp, leggiero and a tied left-hand chord. Relative level stays between −26 and −19 dB from 1:05 to 1:35 (with a boundary of 0.40 at 1:14), then rises to −11.0 dB at 1:45. The start of the section is approximate.

cues.title: On the programme, winter 1920–21
cues.text: Rachmaninoff paired the Barcarolle with Polichinelle in recitals in Cleveland (15 November 1920), Buffalo, Toronto and Montclair, New Jersey. He played it alone at Carnegie Hall on 19 December 1920.
cues.evidence: The recital programmes are listed in the Classical Pianists chronology of Rachmaninoff: https://classical-pianists.net/vii-b/sergei-rachmaninoff/chronology-2/ (15 and 23 November, 8 and 19 December 1920; 12 January 1921). The listing is a reconstruction from programmes and press; it does not say whether the pieces were encores.

cues.title: The record’s loudest stretch
cues.text: Near 2:05–2:15 the record reaches its loudest point, with attacks at seven a second. The score has a Presto marked pppp that swells to f and falls to pp; the strongest boundary of the file follows at 2:22.
cues.evidence: The level reaches −5.8 dB at 2:10 and −6.3 dB at 2:15 with 7.4 and 6.0 attacks per second; a boundary of 0.89 falls at 2:08 and 1.00 at 2:22; the level is −15.8 dB at 2:20. The score’s fifth and sixth pages show Presto, pppp, a hairpin crescendo to f, dim. and pp. The start of the Presto is not located.

cues.title: The tune comes back
cues.text: At about 2:22 the Allegro moderato restores the opening texture: a left-hand tune at mf under a swaying right hand, after the Presto has died away. Compare it with the first minute.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary (1.00) falls at 2:22, with the level at −15.8 dB at 2:20 after −6.3 dB at 2:15. The sixth page of the score marks Allegro moderato (ppp, then mf) with a left-hand melody under a right-hand rocking figure like that on the first page.

cues.title: Edison’s only disc of it
cues.text: Edison issued the Barcarolle on Diamond Disc 82202 in February 1921, nearly two years after the sessions, coupled with Chopin’s Waltz in A♭, Op. 64 No. 3. It is Rachmaninoff’s only disc of the piece; the RCA reissue uses take C, one of three.
cues.evidence: Richard Densmore’s Edison list gives 82202 as 2/1921 and DAHR catalogues the disc with the Chopin waltz: https://www.densmore-edisondd.info/EdisonRecordsList/index.html and https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/objects/refer/234970. The RCA booklet’s discography lists a single Barcarolle, Edison 6743-C (CD 10, track 16), and says Edison issued all three takes: https://archive.org/details/9-0023-sergei-rachmaninoff-complete-recordings-booklet-to-10-cd-set-rca-bmg-09026-61265-2-1992

cues.title: Slower, then a rising climax
cues.text: From about 3:00 the score marks Meno mosso, a slower passage. From about 3:16 a Con moto figure rises over chords and swells to a second loud stretch around 3:30.
cues.evidence: Boundaries of 0.53 at 3:00 and 0.38–0.39 at 3:16–3:20; attacks rise from 3.0 to 6.2–7.2 per second at 3:15–3:20; level reaches −11.5 and −10.4 dB at 3:30–3:35. The score’s eighth page marks Meno mosso and its ninth page Con moto, ppp, with a crescendo to f.

cues.title: Down to pppp
cues.text: After the climax the figures thin and the level falls. The score marks dim., then rising sextuplets in the highest octave at pppp, and two soft closing chords. In this record the sound has faded by 3:55.
cues.evidence: A boundary of 0.57 falls at 3:34; level falls from −10.4 dB at 3:35 to −27.5 dB at 3:45 and −42.4 dB at 3:50, with silence by 3:55. The score’s tenth page shows dim., pppp sextuplets in 8va and two closing chords (ppp, pp).

transitions.title: The tune gives way to a quick figure
transitions.how: The Moderato material dies away. Con moto then replaces its swaying thirds with a continuous sixteenth-note figure at ppp, marked leggiero, over a held chord that has moved into the treble clef. Tempo, figuration and register change together, and the marking drops from the opening’s pp to ppp.
transitions.evidence: The bottom of the score’s third page marks Con moto, ppp, leggiero with a tied chord in the left hand’s treble clef. The analysis shows a boundary of 0.40 at 1:14, with the level between −26 and −19 dB. The boundary is a soft one, so the time is approximate.

transitions.title: Presto, climax, then the tune
transitions.how: Later the score marks a Presto at pppp whose crescendo reaches f and then falls back through dim. to pp. The Allegro moderato that follows brings back the opening’s texture, a left-hand tune under a swaying right hand, at ppp and then mf. Level and tempo settle before the theme returns, so the tune is restated more quietly after the climax.
transitions.evidence: The record reaches its loudest windows at 2:10 and 2:15 (−5.8 and −6.3 dB; 2:05 is −9.0 dB), a boundary of 0.89 falls at 2:08, and the strongest boundary (1.00) falls at 2:22 with the level at −15.8 dB at 2:20. The score’s fifth and sixth pages show Presto, a hairpin to f, dim., pp and Allegro moderato.

transitions.title: The theme slows
transitions.how: The pages before the Meno mosso mark dim., pp and ppp. At Meno mosso the right hand keeps slurred sixteenth-note figures at a slower tempo while the left hand holds chords. Tempo slows and the level stays low, so the section opens quietly after the returning theme.
transitions.evidence: A boundary of 0.53 falls at 3:00 and the level is −22.5 dB at 2:55. The score’s eighth page shows pp, ppp and Meno mosso in the middle of the page. Bar numbers are not assigned.

transitions.title: Slower, then a rising Con moto
transitions.how: After the Meno mosso the score marks Con moto, ppp, with continuous sixteenth-note figures over long chords. A crescendo to f follows, with chords in the left hand and fast figures in the right. Tempo quickens and the dynamic rises from ppp to f.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries of 0.38–0.39 fall at 3:16–3:20; attacks rise from 3.0 per second at 3:10 to 6.2–7.2 at 3:15–3:20, and the level reaches −10.4 dB at 3:35. The ninth page of the score begins Con moto at ppp and reaches f.

transitions.title: The climax falls to pppp
transitions.how: The second Con moto’s f chords give way to a dim. The tenth page shows sixteenth-note figures over chords, then pppp sextuplets in the highest octave, and a last pair of soft chords (ppp, pp). Level falls and the register rises together, so the piece ends in its thinnest sound.
transitions.evidence: A boundary of 0.57 falls at 3:34; the level falls from −10.4 dB at 3:35 to −42.4 dB at 3:50, with silence by 3:55. The score’s tenth page shows dim., pppp sextuplets in 8va and two closing chords.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Solo piano, performed by the composer
fields.note: No performing score edition is identified, and the printed text is not asserted to match the performance.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Sources agree on April 1919 and disagree on the day. The Archive filenames, the RCA register and the Library of Congress bulletin give 23 April; DAHR’s Edison ledger entry and the Classical Pianists chronology give 24 April. The day is not resolved here.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: DAHR gives New York for every take. The Library of Congress bulletin names Edison Studios, New York. The label place of publication, Orange, New Jersey, is not the session place.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Edison is the original label (released at Orange, New Jersey, according to DAHR’s label record); the uploader identifies the 1992 RCA/BMG set as the immediate source of the file.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Edison Diamond Disc 82202 (10-inch double-faced; Barcarolle on side L, Chopin’s Valse in A♭, Op. 64 No. 3, on side R); RCA-BMG 09026 61265 2, CD 10 (1992)
fields.note: The side assignment and disc number are documented by the Edison list and the Library of Congress bulletin; the disc used for the 1992 transfer is not identified. DAHR’s MARC record for the disc gives 10-inch, 80 rpm and a bracketed publication year of [1919], which predates the release documented by Densmore (February 1921) and by the Library of Congress ([1921]) and is not followed for the release date; either year is before 1926.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The RCA register names Edison 6743-C for CD 10, track 16, and the Archive file is that track. Edison issued all three takes (A, B, C) on the same catalogue number, so the disc number alone does not identify the take, and no comparison of takes was made. DAHR gives its own take dates (24 April 1919) which differ from the RCA register (23 April).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: John Pfeiffer, reissue producer; Ward Marston, disc-to-DAT transfer; André Gauthier, remastering supervisor; Anthony Salvatore, remastering engineer
fields.note: These are the credits printed for the 1992 RCA/BMG set. Their connection to this access file rests on the uploader’s identification of the item as CD 10 of that set. The later ripper and uploader are not named as engineers.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The set was issued in 1992, but the dates of the disc-to-DAT transfer, the remastering and the later CD extraction are not stated. The Internet Archive upload of 11 October 2025 is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Disc-to-DAT transfer, then digital remastering at BMG/RCA Studios, New York City; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV.
fields.note: The booklet says surface imperfections were reduced without radical removal of all surface noise. It gives no equalisation, pitch-correction, noise-reduction or editing settings, and none is inferred from the audio analysis. The booklet’s essay says the Edison engineer evidently placed the upright piano too far from the recording horns, so the sound is distant.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Rachmaninoff died in 1943. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: US public domain: the issued sound recording was published by 1925 (Edison Diamond Disc 82202, released February 1921).
fields.note: Densmore’s Edison list gives a February 1921 release for 82202, and the Library of Congress Cataloging Service Bulletin 61 catalogues the disc as Edison [1921]; this is independent of the April 1919 session date. The Archive item’s Public Domain Mark is noted but not relied on. The 1992 booklet carries an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any new creative contribution to the mastering is cleared worldwide.

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Interview with Leonard Liebling, The Musical Courier, 1939

composer.background:
Rachmaninoff learnt the sound of Russian worship before he learnt orchestration. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where unaccompanied voices and bells occupied different parts of the ceremony: chant inside the church, metal sounding above and outside it. His music repeatedly brings the two together. A melody moves in narrow steps while bass notes toll beneath it; a chord is struck again before its previous resonance has died. The C♯ minor Prelude, the Second Piano Concerto and The Bells make this audible without requiring an actual church bell. The All-Night Vigil removes the instruments altogether, leaving a choir to produce both the sustained line and the accumulating weight of the harmony.

Born into a landowning family in 1873, he spent his early childhood at Oneg, near Novgorod. His father’s financial failures brought the sale of the estates and a move to St Petersburg. Rachmaninoff entered its Conservatory in 1883, but his general schoolwork deteriorated; his parents separated, and his sister Sofia died of diphtheria. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a transfer to Moscow and the supervision of Nikolai Zverev. The move exchanged a disorganised household for one in which practice, meals and attendance at concerts were regulated by a piano teacher.
composer.epithet: A composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried Russian chant into the concertos and dances of his American exile.
